title: Other Managed Products

brief.h: REIT basics and the pass-through tests
brief.md:
- **REIT** = pool of capital that owns/operates **income-producing real estate** (or real-estate-related assets: mortgages, loans). Modeled on mutual funds: diversification, professional management, share of income, **without buying property directly**.
- Typical holdings: office buildings, malls, apartments, hotels, resorts, self-storage, warehouses, mortgages. Most specialise in **one** property type.
- Low correlation with stocks and bonds → diversification without raising overall volatility.
- **REITs are NOT investment companies** → **not regulated under the Investment Company Act of 1940**.
- **IRS tests for pass-through status (75-75-90):**

| Test | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Assets | **≥ 75% of total assets** in real estate |
| Income | **≥ 75% of gross income** from **rents or mortgage interest** |
| Distribution | **≥ 90% of taxable income** paid to shareholders **annually** as dividends |

- There is **no profitability test** (no “profitable 4 years out of 5” rule).
- If all tests are met, the REIT **passes through gains**; the entity pays tax only on earnings it **does not distribute**. If it distributes 90%+, no corporate tax on the amount passed through.
- **Losses are NOT passed through.** A loss shows up as a **lower share price**.
> **Exam tip** 75-75-90: the first two are 75s (assets, gross income), the 90 is the payout. REITs pass through **income and gains, never losses**.

brief.h: REIT trading: public, non-traded and private
brief.md:
- REITs raise money via an **IPO**; shareholders elect a **board of directors**, which picks investments and hires day-to-day managers.
- Listed REITs trade like **closed-end funds**: they have an NAV but the **market price can be at a premium or discount to NAV** (supply and demand). They are **not** bought/sold at NAV.
- **NAV drivers**: new construction outpacing demand → vacancies up, rents weaken, property values fall → NAV falls. Rising occupancy/property values → share value rises.

| REIT type | Registered under ’33 Act | Exchange-listed | Liquidity / who can buy |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Publicly traded** | Yes | **Yes** | Most liquid; suits retail |
| **Public non-traded** | Yes | **No** | Illiquid; holding periods of **8 years or more** not unusual; limited early redemption; high sales fees |
| **Private** | **No** | No | Exempt from SEC registration and disclosure; **accredited investors and institutions only** |

- Publicly traded and non-traded REITs both file **annual and quarterly reports and a prospectus** with the SEC. The only difference between them: **listed vs not listed**.
- Public REIT investors can buy **common stock, preferred stock or debt securities** through a broker-dealer.
- Private REITs: no disclosure documents → hard to make an informed decision; no liquidity → inappropriate for many.
> **Exam tip** Unless told otherwise, “REIT” means **publicly traded**. It is the right REIT for a retail investor, including one starting with a few shares.

| Type | Invests in | Income comes from |
|---|---|---|
| **Equity REIT** (most common today) | Real property: hospitals, apartments, malls, etc. | **Rent** and **sale of properties** (capital gains) |
| **Mortgage REIT** | **Mortgages and MBS** (commercial and residential) | **Interest** on loans, profit margin on them, sale of mortgages |
| **Hybrid REIT** | **Both** real property and mortgage debt | Rent + capital gains **and** interest |

- Mortgage REITs lend to property owners and also buy existing mortgages/MBS.
- Mortgage REIT risks: **credit risk** and **prepayment risk** (borrowers refinance or repay when rates change); interest-rate changes hit both earnings and asset values.
- Equity REIT risks: weaker demand for space in downturns, falling property values, lower rents; **rising interest rates** raise borrowing costs and hurt profitability.

- REITs that distribute **≥ 90% of taxable income** owe **no corporate tax** on what they pass through → **only shareholder-level tax** (no double taxation).
- **REIT dividends are always taxed as ordinary income** (the investor’s bracket). Dividends from a traditional corporation can get a lower rate if the stock is held **more than 60 days**; REIT dividends never do.
- **No tax shelter**: REITs pass through gains but **not losses**.
- Inside an **IRA** the dividends are not currently taxed (deferred until withdrawal) → REITs can fit an IRA investor seeking income and appreciation.
- **Benefits**: diversification (low correlation, helpful in down markets), **dividends** (steady income; among the most popular equity choices for income investors), **liquidity** (exchange-listed shares), long-term **inflation hedge** for equity REITs.
- **Mortgage REITs**: attractive for potentially **high dividends**.
- **A REIT is appropriate for an investor seeking income.**
> **Exam tip** Income objective → REIT. Tax-shelter objective → DPP (not a REIT).
> **Exam tip** Equity REIT = *rent* and property sales; mortgage REIT = *interest*; hybrid = both.

brief.h: Direct participation programs (DPPs) and tax shelter
brief.md:
- **DPP** = vehicle letting investors take part **directly** in cash flows and **tax benefits** of the underlying business without managing it. The term comes from the **Securities Act of 1933**; SEC and FINRA regulate compensation, fees and expenses in public offerings.
- **Pass-through vehicle**: income, gains, **and losses** flow to investors; the entity itself pays no tax → **no double taxation**.
- DPPs can be **tax shelters**: losses reduce certain taxable income. **Limit: passive losses offset only passive gains** — not ordinary (earned) income or capital gains.
- Pick a DPP for **economic soundness first**, tax benefit second. Investors who do not pay much tax generally should not invest in DPPs.
- **Risks**: often **blind pools** (investments not yet identified → cannot judge risk or return); **highly illiquid**, no guaranteed secondary market.
- Suitable for **institutional and sophisticated (accredited) investors** only; not retail.
- A partnership interest is an **equity security** (an ownership piece of the partnership). Its value tracks the **economic potential of the underlying assets**.
- **S corp** = small-business DPP: income and losses pass through, entity not taxed. **C corps** (Apple, Amazon, etc.) are **not** DPPs: taxed at corporate level and again on dividends.
> **Exam tip** DPP passes through **gains AND losses**; REIT passes through **gains only**.

brief.h: Limited partnership structure and partner roles
brief.md:
- Most common DPP structure: the **limited partnership (LP)**. Examples: **hedge funds, oil and gas programs, real estate programs**.
- Formed by a **partnership agreement** naming the partners and roles, how decisions are made, and how changes/dissolution occur. **Every partner (GP and LP) gets a copy.** It binds the partners together. At least **one GP** is required.

| | General partner (GP) | Limited partner (LP) |
|---|---|---|
| Day-to-day management | **Yes** | **No** (passive) |
| Liability | **Potentially unlimited**, personal | **Limited to amount invested** |

- **GP rights/duties**: bind the partnership to contracts and debt; accept or reject new LPs; charge a management fee; decide **timing and amount of distributions**; **fiduciary duty** to LPs; settle accounts on dissolution.
- **GP prohibitions**: cannot **borrow from the partnership or commingle** personal funds; cannot **compete** with the partnership for personal gain; cannot **continue the partnership after another GP leaves** unless the agreement authorises it.
- **LP rights**: limited liability; **inspect books and records**; **sue the GP** for acting against the partnership’s interest; **vote on significant changes** (“partnership democracy”).
- LP votes are rare, e.g. admit a new GP, contest a judgment against the GP, sale or refinancing of partnership property, allow a GP action contrary to the agreement.
> **Exam tip** LP = passive, limited liability, may inspect books, may sue the GP, may vote on major changes. Running day-to-day business is a GP function.

- Dissolution date is normally set in the partnership agreement; the manager **settles accounts**.
- **Order of claims on liquidation:**

1. **Secured lenders**
2. **Other general creditors** (e.g. unsecured lenders, bondholders)
3. **Limited partners**
4. **General partners** (always **last**, even behind LPs)

- **Taxation**: the LP is **not a taxpayer**. Pass-through to each partner: **income, gains, losses, deductions** (depletion, depreciation). Each partner pays tax on their share → no corporate tax, no double taxation.
- **Depletion** = deduction for using up a **natural resource** (oil, gas). Real estate is not a natural resource, so it **cannot be depleted**.
- **Depreciation** = deduction for loss of value of a **hard (physical) asset**, e.g. buildings. **Raw land is not a hard asset** → no depreciation; raw-land investors seek **appreciation**.
> **Exam tip** Oil and gas → depletion. Real estate buildings → depreciation. Raw land → neither.

brief.h: Master limited partnerships (MLPs) and product comparison
brief.md:
- **MLP** = a limited partnership **offered to the public and traded on exchanges**. Common in natural resources, financial services, real estate; can have hundreds of LPs.
- Features: **freely transferable interests**, **limited liability** (corporation-like) **and** pass-through tax with **no double taxation**.
- Exchange trading → **more liquid and less risky than other DPPs** → suitable for a **wider range of investors, including retail**.
- Tax benefits of an MLP are the **same** as an ordinary LP; the added benefit is **liquidity**.

| Feature | REIT (public) | DPP / LP | MLP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Passes through gains | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Passes through **losses** | **No** | **Yes** (passive) | Yes (passive) |
| Exchange-traded | Yes | **No** | **Yes** |
| Typical investor | Retail OK | Sophisticated / accredited | Retail OK |
| Dividends taxed | Ordinary income, investor level | Pass-through to partner | Pass-through to partner |

> **Exam tip** Not traded on an exchange? Think LP. Public REIT, MLP and ETF all trade on exchanges.

- Set up by a money manager, often as a **limited partnership** (investors cannot lose more than invested). Pooled money, **aggressive trading strategies, little transparency** → generally inappropriate for the average investor.
- **Fees: “two and twenty”** = **1%–2% of assets** annual management fee **plus 20% of profits** (performance fee based on NAV increase). Higher than other funds; can eat returns (some funds need annual gains above 20% for investors to profit after fees and taxes).
- **Regulation**: **exempt from the Investment Company Act of 1940**; historically exempt from ’33 Act registration because sold by **private placement** to institutions and **accredited investors**. **Dodd–Frank (2010)**: advisers managing private funds with **more than $150 million** must **register with the SEC**. Anti-fraud rules apply; managers owe a **fiduciary duty** to fund investors.
- **Strategies**: can invest in anything, even **non-securities** (real estate); use **short selling** (unlimited loss in rising markets) and **leverage** (magnifies losses; forced selling on margin calls). Goal: hedge against declines and give returns **not closely correlated** with stock/bond markets.
- **Buying**: minimums set by each fund, often **$1 million** at the best-known funds. Mostly **open-ended** with additions/withdrawals **monthly or quarterly**. Investor owns a share of **NAV**.
- **Lock-up** = period during which the investor **cannot withdraw**; protects the fund from liquidations and lets managers hold less cash. Creates **liquidity risk**.
- **Prime brokerage**: banks/wealth firms offer bundled services that help consolidate positions across several executing firms.
- Suitable only for **sophisticated, high-net-worth** investors.
> **Exam tip** Short sales + heavy leverage + lock-up = hedge fund. Mutual funds are the opposite: liquid, limited leverage, open to all.

brief.h: Hedge funds vs mutual funds, and private equity
brief.md:
| | Mutual fund | Hedge fund |
|---|---|---|
| Liquidity | Highly liquid, redeemable with issuer | Highly illiquid; lock-up usually **2 years or more** |
| Investments | Securities (incl. derivatives) | Securities **and non-securities** (real estate, jewelry) |
| Leverage | **Limited** ability to trade on margin | **Significant** leverage, incl. derivatives |
| Fees | Expense ratio usually **~1% or less** | **2% management fee plus share of profits** |
| Suitability | All investors, subject to objectives | **High-net-worth and sophisticated only** |

- **Private equity (PE)** firms are typically **limited partnerships** too. Money goes **directly into private companies** (hedge funds focus on securities/alternatives).
- Popular strategy: **buy out or take a majority position** in an underperforming company, install a management team, then **exit** by **taking it public** or **selling** it.
- Manager does the **due diligence** and picks investments; investors are **passive**. Pay: **~2% of invested capital** annually plus **~20% of profits**.
- PE is **one of the riskiest** investments (many companies fail); needs large commitments for **long periods** → only **wealthy individuals and institutions**.
> **Exam tip** PE holds *whole (private) companies*; hedge funds trade *securities and other assets*. Both use the 2-and-20 style fee.

- **Structured product** = return based on one or more underlying securities/markets (single security, basket, index, commodity, bond, currency). Value is derived → can be called **derivatives**. Usually has some guarantee or limit on downside, built with **derivatives and option strategies**. The SIE focus is the **ETN**.
- **ETN** = **unsecured corporate debt**, typically issued by a **broker-dealer**; return is tied to an equity security or market.
- Structure: most of the money is a **bond** (principal protection), the rest a **derivative** giving equity exposure.
- **No interest paid.** If the underlying falls, the investor gets back **principal at maturity but no extra return** → shares **upside, not downside** (as the book describes it).
- **Credit risk**: quality depends on the **issuer’s creditworthiness** (the investment bank), **not** the underlying stock. Issuer default is a risk.
- Exchange-traded but a newer product → **liquidity may be limited**, especially vs other listed securities.

| | ETN | ETF |
|---|---|---|
| Legal form | **Unsecured debt** | Fund that **owns** the securities |
| Owns underlying? | **No** | **Yes** |
| Maturity date | **Yes** | No |
| Secondary market | Much more limited | More liquid |
| Suitability | Narrower (complex) | Wider range of investors |

> **Exam tip** ETN = debt of the issuer. Credit risk of the *issuer*, not the index. The feature an ETN has that an ETF lacks: a **maturity date**.

- **Municipal fund securities** (MSRB Rule D-12): investment **pools similar to mutual funds** but issued by a **state or local government entity**. Professional managers invest for gains and income per a stated objective.
- Unlike ordinary municipal securities, they are **equity, not debt** (investors own a share of the pool).
- **LGIP** (local government investment pool) = vehicle for investing **public funds** held by state/local entities; goal: **safe, liquid, competitive**. Managed by government staff (e.g. state treasurer) or an **outside firm**. Benefits: economies of scale, management, diversification, liquidity.
- **Objectives**: most LGIPs (since the late 1980s) resemble **money market funds**: short-term securities, stability, liquidity, little price volatility. Some LGIPs **maximise return** with longer-term securities → **market and liquidity risk**.
- **Regulation**: technically **municipal securities → regulated by the MSRB**, **not** SEC-registered and **not** under the Investment Company Act of 1940. No prospectus/SAI requirement, **no daily NAV** requirement, **no independent-director board** requirement.
- **Marketing**: usually directly to participants (website). If a **municipal securities dealer** markets it, the dealer must obtain the issuer’s **official statement** and give it to the investor **at or before settlement**.
- **Fees**: annual/misc charges plus manager fee on assets, **paid from pool assets** (lowers returns and share value); a dealer **commission/sales charge** may also apply.
> **Exam tip** LGIP disclosure = **official statement** (not a prospectus). Regulator = **MSRB** (not SEC).

traps: **REIT vs DPP tax treatment.** REITs pass through **gains (income and capital gains) but not losses**; DPPs pass through **both gains and passive losses**. Only DPPs can act as a tax shelter.

**75-75-90 mix-up.** 75% of **total assets** in real estate; 75% of **gross income** from rents/mortgage interest; 90% of **taxable income** distributed. Swapping 75 and 90 (or inventing a profitability test) is the classic wrong choice.
**Public vs non-traded vs private REIT.** Public = registered **and** listed. Non-traded = registered, **not** listed (illiquid, 8+ years). Private = **not** registered, not listed, accredited only.
**REIT price vs NAV.** A listed REIT is not bought at NAV; like a closed-end fund it trades at a **premium or discount** set by supply and demand.
**REIT dividends vs corporate dividends.** REIT dividends are **always ordinary income**; qualified corporate dividends can get a lower rate after holding more than 60 days.
**Equity vs mortgage REIT income.** Equity = **rent and property sales**; mortgage = **interest**; hybrid = both. Mortgage REITs carry **prepayment and credit risk**.
**GP vs LP liability.** GP = potentially **unlimited** personal liability and full management; LP = **limited to investment** and passive.
**Liquidation order.** Secured lenders, general creditors, **limited partners, then general partners last**. People often put GPs ahead of LPs or forget creditors come first.
**Passive losses.** DPP losses are passive and offset only **passive income**, not wages or portfolio gains. Tax benefit should never be the main reason to invest.
**Depletion vs depreciation.** Oil and gas use **depletion** (natural resource); buildings use **depreciation**; **raw land gets neither** (appreciation only).
**LP vs MLP.** An MLP is an LP that is **publicly traded**. Tax benefits are the same; the extra is **liquidity** (and a wider investor base). Limited liability applies to both.
**Two and twenty.** It is **2% of assets (management fee) plus 20% of profits**, not 20% of assets and not a sales charge.

**Hedge fund vs mutual fund.** Hedge funds: private placement, lock-ups, short selling, heavy leverage, non-securities allowed, exempt from the ’40 Act. Mutual funds: liquid, regulated, limited leverage.

**ETN vs ETF.** ETN = **unsecured debt of the issuer** (credit risk, maturity date, does not own the underlying). ETF = owns the securities, no maturity. Credit quality of an ETN follows the **issuer**, not the stock.

**LGIP regulator and document.** Regulated by the **MSRB**, not the SEC; the dealer’s disclosure document is the **official statement**, not a prospectus. Municipal fund securities are **equity**, not debt.

formulas.name: REIT pass-through tests (75-75-90)
formulas.rule: Assets: ≥ 75% of total assets in real estate.  Income: ≥ 75% of gross income from rents or mortgage interest.  Payout: ≥ 90% of taxable income distributed annually.  Pass through gains yes, losses no.
formulas.example: A REIT has taxable income of $10,000,000 and distributes $9,200,000 → 92% ≥ 90%, test met; no corporate tax on the $9.2M passed through. If it distributed only $8,500,000 (85%) it would fail the payout test.

formulas.name: Two and twenty (hedge fund / private equity fee)
formulas.rule: Annual fee = 2% × assets (or invested capital) + 20% × profits.

formulas.name: Liquidation priority in a limited partnership
formulas.rule: 1) Secured lenders → 2) general creditors → 3) limited partners → 4) general partners (last).
formulas.example: Assets of $9M; secured lenders owed $5M, unsecured creditors $3M. Lenders get $5M, creditors $3M, leaving **$1M for LPs**; GPs receive nothing until LPs are made whole.

formulas.name: REIT vs DPP vs MLP decision table
formulas.rule: Losses passed through: REIT no, DPP yes, MLP yes.  Exchange-traded: public REIT yes, DPP no, MLP yes.  Retail suitability: public REIT yes, DPP no, MLP yes.  Goal income → REIT; tax shelter → DPP.
formulas.example: Client wants a liquid, exchange-traded vehicle that passes through partnership income and losses → **MLP**. Client wants steady dividends from real estate with no losses passed through → **publicly traded REIT**.

formulas.name: Which tax deduction applies?
formulas.rule: Natural resource (oil, gas) → depletion.  Hard asset (building, equipment) → depreciation.  Raw land → no deduction, appreciation only.
formulas.example: An LP owns an apartment building, a gas well and a parcel of undeveloped land: building = depreciation, well = depletion, land = neither.

cards.f: What is a REIT?
cards.b: A pool that owns/operates **income-producing real estate** or related assets, giving diversification and dividends without buying property directly.

cards.f: Is a REIT regulated under the Investment Company Act of 1940?
cards.b: **No.** REITs are not investment companies.

cards.f: REIT asset test
cards.b: At least **75% of total assets** invested in real estate.

cards.f: REIT gross income test
cards.b: At least **75% of gross income** from rents or mortgage interest.

cards.f: REIT distribution test
cards.b: Distribute at least **90% of taxable income** to shareholders annually as dividends.

cards.f: Is there a profitability test for REIT pass-through status?
cards.b: **No.** Only the 75% asset, 75% income and 90% distribution tests.

cards.f: Can a REIT pass through losses?
cards.b: **No.** It passes through income and gains only; losses show up as a **lower share price**.

cards.f: What happens to REIT earnings it does not distribute?
cards.b: The corporate entity **pays tax** on them.

cards.f: How do listed REIT shares price relative to NAV?
cards.b: At a **premium or discount**, set by supply and demand (like closed-end funds).

cards.f: Effect of new construction outrunning demand on a REIT
cards.b: Vacancies rise, rents weaken, property values fall → **NAV decreases**.

cards.f: Publicly traded REIT: registered and listed?
cards.b: **Registered under the ’33 Act: yes. Exchange-listed: yes.**

cards.f: Non-traded REIT: registered and listed?
cards.b: **Registered: yes. Listed: no.** Generally illiquid.

cards.f: Private REIT: registered and listed?
cards.b: **Neither.** Exempt from SEC registration; no exchange trading.

cards.f: Who may buy a private REIT?
cards.b: **Accredited investors and institutional clients** only.

cards.f: Which REIT is most appropriate for retail investors?
cards.b: The **publicly traded** REIT (exchange-traded, most liquid). It is the default meaning of “REIT”.

cards.f: Most common REIT type today
cards.b: **Equity REITs.**

cards.f: How does an equity REIT earn revenue?
cards.b: **Rent** from properties and **sale of properties**.

cards.f: What does a mortgage REIT hold and earn?
cards.b: **Mortgages/MBS**; earns mainly **interest**, margin and sales of mortgages.

cards.f: Hybrid REIT
cards.b: Combines equity and mortgage strategies: real property **and** mortgage debt; earns rent, gains **and** interest.

cards.f: Two risks specific to mortgage REITs
cards.b: **Credit risk** and **prepayment risk** (borrowers refinance or repay as rates change).

cards.f: How are REIT dividends taxed?
cards.b: Always as **ordinary income** at the investor’s bracket; only taxed at shareholder level.

cards.f: Do REITs get the lower rate that qualified corporate dividends can get?
cards.b: **No.** The lower rate requires holding a traditional corporation’s stock more than 60 days; REIT dividends are always ordinary income.

cards.f: Can a REIT serve as a tax shelter?
cards.b: **No.** Losses are not passed through.

cards.f: Investor objective best matched to a REIT
cards.b: **Income** (dividends); also long-term income plus appreciation.

cards.f: What is a direct participation program?
cards.b: Vehicle letting investors share directly in **cash flows and tax benefits** of a business without managing it.

cards.f: What can DPP passive losses offset?
cards.b: Only **passive gains**, not ordinary income or capital gains.

cards.f: What should be the primary factor in choosing a DPP?
cards.b: **Economic soundness**, not tax benefit.

cards.f: DPPs vs REITs: which passes through losses?
cards.b: **DPPs** pass through gains and passive losses; REITs pass through gains only.

cards.f: Suitable investors for DPPs
cards.b: **Institutional and sophisticated (accredited)** investors, because of high risk and illiquidity.

cards.f: Most common DPP business structure
cards.b: The **limited partnership**.

cards.f: S corporation and DPPs
cards.b: An S corp is a **DPP** for small business: income and losses pass through, entity untaxed.

cards.f: Why is a C corp not a DPP?
cards.b: It is a **taxable entity**; dividends are taxed at corporate and again at shareholder level.

cards.f: GP management role and liability
cards.b: Manages day-to-day with full authority; **potentially unlimited personal liability**.

cards.f: LP liability
cards.b: **Limited to the amount invested**; no day-to-day management.

cards.f: What document forms a limited partnership?
cards.b: The **partnership agreement**; all partners (GP and LP) must receive a copy.

cards.f: Name four GP rights
cards.b: Bind partnership to contracts/debt; **accept or reject new LPs**; charge a management fee; set **timing and amount of distributions**.

cards.f: GP fiduciary duty
cards.b: Act in the **best interest of the limited partners** when investing and managing.

cards.f: Three things a GP cannot do
cards.b: **Borrow from or commingle** funds with the partnership; **compete** against it; continue it after another GP leaves unless the agreement allows.

cards.f: When do limited partners vote?
cards.b: Rarely: new GP, contesting a judgment against the GP, sale/refinancing of property, GP action contrary to the agreement (“partnership democracy”).

cards.f: Liquidation order of an LP
cards.b: **Secured lenders → general creditors → limited partners → general partners.**

cards.f: Who is last in line when an LP dissolves?
cards.b: The **general partner**, behind even the limited partners.

cards.f: What flows through to LP partners for tax?
cards.b: Income, gains, losses and deductions (depletion, depreciation); the **partnership is not a taxpayer**.

cards.f: Depletion deduction applies to…
cards.b: **Natural resources** such as oil and gas; not real estate.

cards.f: Depreciation applies to…
cards.b: **Hard assets** that lose value over time; **raw land** gets no depreciation.

cards.f: Master limited partnership
cards.b: An LP **offered to the public and traded on exchanges**.

cards.f: MLP advantages over a regular LP
cards.b: **Liquidity** (exchange-traded, freely transferable interests); tax benefits are the same.

cards.f: Two and twenty means…
cards.b: **2% annual management fee** plus **20% of profits**. Management fee is 1%-2% of assets.

cards.f: Hedge fund regulation under the ’40 Act
cards.b: **Exempt** from the Investment Company Act of 1940.

cards.f: Dodd–Frank threshold for hedge fund registration
cards.b: Private funds with more than **$150 million** in assets must register with the SEC.

cards.f: Hedge fund risks from short selling and leverage
cards.b: Shorts can lose an **unlimited** amount; leverage magnifies losses and forces selling on margin calls.

cards.f: Typical minimum investment at well-known hedge funds
cards.b: About **$1 million**.

cards.f: Lock-up period
cards.b: Time when investors **cannot withdraw**; creates **liquidity risk**; lets managers hold less cash.

cards.f: Hedge fund suitability
cards.b: Only **sophisticated, high-net-worth** investors.

cards.f: Mutual fund vs hedge fund liquidity
cards.b: Mutual fund: redeemable with issuer. Hedge fund: **lock-up usually 2 years or more**.

cards.f: Private equity vs hedge fund investment focus
cards.b: PE invests **directly in private companies**; hedge funds in securities and alternatives.

cards.f: Classic private equity strategy
cards.b: Buy out or take a majority of an **underperforming company**, rebuild management, then **IPO or sell**.

cards.f: Private equity manager compensation
cards.b: About **2% of invested capital** annually plus about **20% of profits**.

cards.f: What is a structured product?
cards.b: Product whose return is based on underlying securities/markets, usually with limited downside, built with **derivatives and options**.

cards.f: What is an ETN?
cards.b: **Unsecured corporate debt**, typically issued by a **broker-dealer**, tied to an equity security or market.

cards.f: ETN structure
cards.b: Mostly a **bond** for principal protection plus a **derivative** for equity exposure.

cards.f: Does an ETN pay interest?
cards.b: **No.** If the underlying falls, the investor gets back **principal at maturity** with no extra return.

cards.f: ETN credit risk depends on…
cards.b: The **issuer’s creditworthiness**, not the underlying stock.

cards.f: ETN feature an ETF lacks
cards.b: A **maturity date**.

cards.f: Do ETFs or ETNs own the underlying securities?
cards.b: **ETFs do; ETNs do not** (they are unsecured debt).

cards.f: Municipal fund security
cards.b: Investment pool like a mutual fund, issued by a **state or local government**; defined in **MSRB Rule D-12**.

cards.f: Are municipal fund securities debt or equity?
cards.b: **Equity** (a share in the pool).

cards.f: LGIP purpose
cards.b: Invest public funds of governments: **safe, liquid, competitive**.

cards.f: Who regulates LGIPs?
cards.b: The **MSRB**; no SEC registration, not under the ’40 Act.

cards.f: Mutual fund requirements LGIPs do not have
cards.b: Prospectus/SAI, **daily NAV** calculation, board with independent directors.

cards.f: Document a dealer must give an LGIP investor
cards.b: The issuer’s **official statement**, at or before settlement.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the IRS tests a REIT must meet to pass income through to shareholders?
o: At least 75% of gross income must come from rents or mortgage interest
At least 90% of total assets must be invested in real estate
At least 75% of taxable income must be distributed each year
The REIT must show a profit in four of every five years
w: Correct: the income test requires at least 75% of gross income to be derived from rents or mortgage interest on real estate.
Wrong: the asset test is 75% of total assets in real estate, not 90%; the 90% figure belongs to distributions.
Wrong: the distribution test is 90% of taxable income, so 75% is the wrong figure for payout.
Wrong: there is no profitability test of any kind in the REIT pass-through requirements.

questions.q: Which statement about the regulation of REITs is correct?
o: They are regulated as open-end investment companies under the Investment Company Act of 1940
They must calculate NAV daily and redeem shares on demand
They must have a board made up entirely of independent directors
They are not investment companies and are not regulated under the Investment Company Act of 1940
w: Wrong: REITs are not investment companies, so the 1940 Act does not apply to them as open-end funds.
Wrong: daily NAV calculation and redemption on demand describe open-end mutual funds, not REITs, which trade on exchanges.
Wrong: the independent-director board is a 1940 Act requirement for funds; REITs elect an ordinary board of directors.
Correct: REITs are not investment companies, so the Investment Company Act of 1940 does not govern them.

questions.q: A REIT reports taxable income of $8,000,000 for the year. What is the minimum amount it must distribute to shareholders to keep its pass-through status?
w: Wrong: $6,000,000 is 75% of taxable income, which is the asset and income test percentage, not the payout test.
Wrong: $7,600,000 is 95% of taxable income, a figure that does not appear in the REIT requirements.
Correct: the distribution test requires 90% of taxable income, so 0.90 × $8,000,000 = $7,200,000.
Wrong: distributing 100% would satisfy the test but is not the minimum; only 90% is required.

questions.q: Which of the following does a REIT that meets all IRS requirements pass through to its shareholders?
o: Income, capital gains and losses
Income and capital gains, but not losses
Capital losses only
Losses and deductions but not gains
w: Wrong: losses are not passed through by a REIT; that feature belongs to direct participation programs.
Correct: REITs pass through income and gains; losses are not passed through and instead lower the share price.
Wrong: a REIT never passes capital losses to shareholders, who see losses only as lower share price.
Wrong: this reverses the rule; REITs pass through gains and income, not losses or deductions.

questions.q: A publicly traded REIT’s shares usually trade at
o: a price set by supply and demand, which may be above or below NAV
exactly net asset value per share
net asset value plus a front-end sales charge
net asset value less a redemption fee
w: Correct: like closed-end fund shares, listed REIT shares trade at a market price that can be at a premium or discount to NAV.
Wrong: only open-end funds are priced at NAV; exchange-traded REIT shares are priced by the market.
Wrong: a front-end sales charge on NAV is an open-end mutual fund feature, not how listed REIT shares trade.
Wrong: redemption at NAV less a fee is an open-end fund feature; REIT holders sell on the exchange instead.

questions.q: A REIT owns suburban office buildings. A wave of new office construction opens in the same markets faster than tenants can absorb it. What is the most likely effect on the REIT?
o: Occupancy rises and the share price rises
The REIT must pass the resulting losses through to shareholders
The REIT loses its exemption from the Investment Company Act
Vacancy rates rise, rents weaken and the REIT’s net asset value falls
w: Wrong: when supply outruns demand, occupancy falls rather than rises, which hurts the share price.
Wrong: REITs cannot pass losses through; the weakness shows up as a lower share price instead.
Wrong: REITs are never covered by the 1940 Act, so there is no exemption to lose from market conditions.
Correct: oversupply raises vacancies and pressures rents and property values, so NAV declines.

questions.q: Which type of REIT is registered with the SEC but is NOT listed on an exchange?
o: Publicly traded REIT
Private REIT
Public non-traded REIT
Hybrid REIT listed on Nasdaq
w: Wrong: a publicly traded REIT is both registered with the SEC and exchange-listed, unlike this one.
Wrong: a private REIT is neither registered nor listed; it is exempt from SEC registration.
Correct: a non-traded REIT is registered under the 1933 Act and files reports, but its shares do not trade on an exchange.
Wrong: a REIT listed on Nasdaq is exchange-traded by definition, regardless of whether it is a hybrid.

questions.q: A retired client with modest savings wants a small real estate position she can sell quickly if she needs cash. Which REIT should a representative suggest?
o: A private REIT
A publicly traded REIT
A public non-traded REIT
A REIT that restricts early redemption for eight years
w: Wrong: private REITs are sold only to accredited investors and institutions and have no secondary market.
Correct: only a publicly traded REIT offers exchange liquidity and is the appropriate REIT for a retail investor.
Wrong: non-traded REITs are generally illiquid, with limited early redemption and high fees.
Wrong: an eight-year restriction is the opposite of the quick liquidity the client requires.

questions.q: Which of the following is true of private REITs?
o: They are generally exempt from SEC registration and may be sold only to accredited investors and institutions
They file annual and quarterly reports and a prospectus with the SEC
They are listed on the major exchanges
They are the most appropriate REIT for retail investors
w: Correct: private REITs are exempt from SEC registration and disclosure and are limited to accredited and institutional buyers.
Wrong: annual and quarterly reports and a prospectus are required of public and non-traded REITs, not private ones.
Wrong: private REITs do not trade on exchanges; listing is what separates public REITs.
Wrong: publicly traded REITs, not private ones, are the most appropriate REIT form for retail clients.

questions.q: Compared with a publicly traded REIT, a public non-traded REIT
o: is exempt from SEC disclosure filings
is sold only to accredited investors
trades at a daily premium or discount to NAV on an exchange
files the same SEC disclosures but is generally illiquid and may lock up money for eight years or more
w: Wrong: non-traded REITs are registered and subject to the same disclosure filings as public REITs.
Wrong: the accredited-only restriction applies to private REITs; non-traded REITs are publicly distributed through broker-dealers.
Wrong: exchange trading at a premium or discount describes listed REITs; non-traded shares are not on an exchange.
Correct: both are SEC-registered with reports and a prospectus; the difference is non-traded shares are not listed and are illiquid.

questions.q: A REIT whose revenue comes mainly from rent on the buildings it owns and from selling those buildings is a(n)
o: mortgage REIT
hybrid REIT
equity REIT
private REIT
w: Wrong: mortgage REITs earn mainly interest on mortgage loans and mortgage-backed securities.
Wrong: hybrid REITs combine property ownership and mortgage holdings, earning both rent and interest.
Correct: equity REITs own and operate real property and earn rent and gains from sales of properties.
Wrong: private describes registration status, not the source of the REIT’s income.

questions.q: A REIT holds hospitals, a mortgage portfolio on apartment buildings, and receives both rent and interest. How is it classified?
o: Equity REIT
Hybrid REIT
Mortgage REIT
Master limited partnership
w: Wrong: an equity REIT holds only real property and earns rent and property-sale gains.
Correct: holding both real property and mortgage debt, with income from rent and interest, defines a hybrid REIT.
Wrong: a mortgage REIT holds only mortgages and MBS; this REIT also owns real property.
Wrong: an MLP is a publicly traded limited partnership, not a REIT.

questions.q: Which statement about mortgage REITs is correct?
o: Their earnings and asset values are exposed to credit risk and prepayment risk
They earn most of their revenue from rent
They are the most common REIT type today
They pass through losses to investors
w: Correct: mortgage REITs hold loans whose borrowers may default or refinance and repay early when rates change.
Wrong: rent is the main income source for equity REITs; mortgage REITs earn interest.
Wrong: equity REITs are the most common type today, not mortgage REITs, so this statement is false.
Wrong: no REIT passes losses through to its shareholders; losses only lower the share price.

questions.q: Dividends paid by a REIT to its shareholders are generally taxed
o: at the lower rate if held more than 60 days
as a tax-free return of capital in all cases
at the corporate level only, not to the shareholder
as ordinary income at the shareholder’s tax bracket
w: Wrong: the lower rate with a 60-day holding period applies to dividends of traditional corporations, not REITs.
Wrong: REIT dividends are not tax-free; they are taxed as ordinary income.
Wrong: a qualifying REIT avoids corporate tax on what it distributes; the shareholder bears the tax.
Correct: because the REIT passes through gains and avoids corporate tax, its dividends are always taxed as ordinary income to the investor.

questions.q: A client in a high tax bracket wants an investment that will pass through real estate losses to reduce her taxes. A publicly traded REIT is
o: suitable, because REITs pass through gains and losses
suitable, because losses offset her wages
not suitable for that purpose, because REITs do not pass through losses
suitable only if she holds shares more than 60 days
w: Wrong: REITs pass through gains and income only, never losses, so no shelter is available.
Wrong: no REIT losses reach the investor, so there is nothing to offset against wages.
Correct: REITs offer no tax shelter because losses stay inside the trust and show up as a lower price per share.
Wrong: the 60-day holding period concerns dividend tax rates and has no connection to loss pass-through.

questions.q: Which investor objective is a REIT most appropriate for?
o: Tax shelter through loss pass-through
Current income
Capital preservation with a guaranteed return
Avoiding all market risk
w: Wrong: tax shelter is a DPP feature; REITs do not pass losses through.
Correct: REITs are among the most popular equity choices for investors whose primary objective is current income.
Wrong: REITs carry real estate market and interest-rate risk and offer no guarantee.
Wrong: REIT values fall with property values and rising rates, so market risk remains.

questions.q: A client invests in an equity REIT. Which development poses the GREATEST threat to the REIT’s profitability according to the chapter?
o: A rise in interest rates that increases the REIT’s borrowing costs
An increase in occupancy rates across its buildings
A rise in demand for new space
A decline in the REIT’s correlation with stocks and bonds
w: Correct: higher interest rates raise borrowing costs and can drive down an equity REIT’s profitability.
Wrong: rising occupancy lifts rents and property values, which helps rather than hurts the REIT.
Wrong: greater demand for space supports rents and values, which benefits the REIT.
Wrong: low correlation is a diversification benefit, not a threat to profitability.

questions.q: A 40-year-old client with an IRA wants income and appreciation and is comfortable with real estate risk. Which statement best supports recommending a publicly traded REIT inside the IRA?
o: REIT losses will offset other IRA income
The IRA will receive the lower qualified dividend rate
REITs are guaranteed not to fall in value
The REIT dividends are not currently taxed inside the IRA; tax is deferred until withdrawal
w: Wrong: REITs do not pass through losses, so there is nothing to offset against other IRA income.
Wrong: REIT dividends are always ordinary income and never earn the lower qualified rate.
Wrong: REIT shares can fall with property values, interest rates and demand.
Correct: the IRA shelters the ordinary-income dividends, which are deferred until the client withdraws.

questions.q: Which managed product can potentially serve as a tax shelter because it passes losses through to investors?
o: Publicly traded REIT
Exchange-traded note
Direct participation program
Local government investment pool
w: Wrong: REITs pass through gains but not losses and cannot shelter income.
Wrong: an ETN is unsecured debt of its issuer and passes through no losses.
Correct: DPPs pass through income, gains and passive losses, so they can shelter certain taxable income.
Wrong: an LGIP is a municipal fund security and offers no tax shelter through losses.

questions.q: Losses passed through to an investor in a direct participation program may be used to offset
o: wages and salary
passive income only
capital gains from stock sales
any type of taxable income
w: Wrong: wages are ordinary (earned) income, which cannot be offset by passive losses.
Correct: passive losses can only offset passive gains, which limits the tax-shelter benefit of a DPP.
Wrong: capital gains are not passive income, so DPP losses cannot be applied to them.
Wrong: the offset is restricted to passive gains, not all taxable income.

questions.q: A direct participation program described as a blind pool is one that
o: does not disclose the specific investments it will make
does not disclose the investors’ names to the SEC
is prohibited from selling any assets in its first five years
does not require investors to disclose their income
w: Correct: in a blind pool the specific business activities or holdings are not yet identified, so investors cannot evaluate risk or return.
Wrong: a blind pool concerns hidden investments, not the privacy of the investors’ identities.
Wrong: no five-year asset-sale prohibition defines a blind pool; the term is about undisclosed holdings.
Wrong: investor income disclosure has nothing to do with the term blind pool.

questions.q: Which of the following are reasons DPPs are generally suitable only for sophisticated investors? I. Frequent blind-pool structure II. Highly illiquid with no guaranteed secondary market III. Daily redemption at NAV IV. High risk
o: I and II only
II and III only
I, III and IV only
I, II and IV only
w: Wrong: this omits high risk, which the chapter also cites as a reason for limited suitability.
Wrong: daily redemption at NAV is an open-end fund feature, so statement III cannot be a DPP risk.
Wrong: statement III is false for DPPs and this choice drops the illiquidity point, so it cannot be correct.
Correct: blind pools, illiquidity and high risk all limit suitability, while daily NAV redemption is not a DPP feature.

questions.q: The most common business structure used for a direct participation program is the
o: C corporation
open-end investment company
limited partnership
unit investment trust
w: Wrong: a C corporation is taxable and subject to double taxation, so it is not a DPP.
Wrong: an open-end investment company is a mutual fund, which is not a DPP.
Correct: the limited partnership is the most common form, with general and limited partners.
Wrong: a unit investment trust is an investment company product and not the usual DPP structure.

questions.q: A client owns shares in a small business organized as an S corporation. Compared with a client who owns Apple stock, the S corporation shareholder
o: pays tax only at the corporate level
receives a pass-through of income and losses and is not subject to double taxation
is subject to double taxation on dividends
cannot deduct any losses of the business
w: Wrong: the S corp entity is not taxed at all; tax is paid by the shareholder on the passed-through amounts.
Correct: an S corp is a type of DPP, so income and losses pass through to shareholders and the entity itself is not taxed.
Wrong: double taxation is the C corporation problem, as with Apple, not the S corporation.
Wrong: losses pass through to S corp shareholders just as they do for other DPPs.

questions.q: Which of the following is a general partner in a limited partnership?
o: The partner who manages the business and may have unlimited personal liability
The passive investor whose liability is limited to the amount invested
The partner who is paid ahead of all creditors on dissolution
The partner who is prohibited from making any decision
w: Correct: general partners actively manage and usually bear personal liability along with all management authority.
Wrong: that describes a limited partner, who is passive and has liability limited to the investment.
Wrong: general partners are paid last, not ahead of creditors, and management authority and liability define them.
Wrong: general partners hold the management authority, so they are not barred from decisions.

questions.q: Which document binds the partners of a limited partnership together and describes the roles of the general and limited partners?
o: Articles of incorporation
Corporate resolution
Prospectus
Partnership agreement
w: Wrong: articles of incorporation create a corporation, not a partnership, so they do not apply here.
Wrong: a corporate resolution authorizes actions of a corporation, not partners in an LP.
Wrong: a prospectus is an offering document for investors, not the agreement that governs partner roles.
Correct: the partnership agreement names the partners and roles and defines how the partnership operates and dissolves.

questions.q: Which statement about the partnership agreement is correct?
o: Only the general partners receive a copy
Only the limited partners receive a copy
Every partner, both general and limited, must receive a copy
It is optional if the partnership has fewer than ten limited partners
w: Wrong: limited partners also receive a copy, since the agreement defines their rights and roles.
Wrong: general partners also receive it; the agreement is not restricted to the limited partners.
Correct: all partners, general and limited, must be given a copy of the partnership agreement.
Wrong: establishing an LP requires a partnership agreement, and no exemption based on investor count exists.

questions.q: An interest in a limited partnership is classified as
o: a debt security, because the partner lends money to the business
an equity security, because the partner owns a piece of the partnership
a municipal fund security
a money market instrument
w: Wrong: limited partners are owners, not creditors, so the interest is not debt.
Correct: a partner holds an ownership stake, so the interest is an equity security.
Wrong: municipal fund securities are pools issued by government entities, not business partnerships.
Wrong: a money market instrument is short-term debt, which does not describe an ownership interest.

questions.q: Which of the following is a RIGHT of a general partner?
o: Determining the timing and amount of cash distributions
Competing against the partnership for personal gain
Borrowing money from the partnership
Mixing personal funds with partnership funds
w: Correct: the general partner decides when and how much cash is distributed, along with rights to bind the partnership and charge a fee.
Wrong: competing with the partnership for personal gain is expressly prohibited for a general partner.
Wrong: borrowing from the partnership is a prohibited activity for general partners.
Wrong: commingling personal and partnership funds is something a general partner is prohibited from doing.

questions.q: All of the following are limited partner rights EXCEPT the right to
o: inspect the books and records of the partnership
sue the general partner for acting against the partnership’s interest
vote on significant changes to the partnership
bind the partnership to legal contracts
w: Wrong: inspecting the books and records is a recognized limited partner right.
Wrong: limited partners may sue the general partner if its actions are not in the partnership’s best interest.
Wrong: voting on significant changes, called partnership democracy, is a limited partner right.
Correct: binding the partnership to contracts and debt is a general partner right; limited partners are passive.

questions.q: The general partner of a real estate LP proposes selling the partnership’s main building at a price the limited partners believe is too low. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Limited partners have no rights because they are passive investors
Limited partners can personally run the building’s day-to-day operations
Limited partners can vote on the sale of partnership property and may sue if the general partner acts against the partnership’s interest
The general partner may sell freely because limited partners may only inspect books
w: Wrong: passive investors still hold voting, inspection and suit rights, so they are not powerless.
Wrong: limited partners do not take part in day-to-day management, as they are passive investors.
Correct: sale or refinancing of partnership property is a matter on which limited partners vote, and they can sue a general partner who breaches duties.
Wrong: inspection is only one limited partner right; they also vote on a sale of property.

questions.q: A general partner in an LP is NOT permitted to
o: charge the partnership a management fee
continue the partnership after another general partner leaves unless the agreement authorizes it
accept or reject new limited partners
settle accounts upon dissolution
w: Wrong: charging a management fee for overseeing the partnership is a general partner right.
Correct: continuing after a GP’s departure is restricted unless the partnership agreement has authorized it.
Wrong: accepting or rejecting new limited partners is a general partner right.
Wrong: settling accounts upon dissolution of the partnership is a duty of the general partner.

questions.q: In the liquidation of a limited partnership, which group is paid LAST?
o: General partners
Limited partners
General creditors
Secured lenders
w: Correct: general partners are last in line, behind lenders, creditors and even the limited partners.
Wrong: limited partners are paid ahead of general partners but after creditors.
Wrong: general creditors are paid after secured lenders but before any partners.
Wrong: secured lenders are first in line for payment, so they are certainly not paid last.

questions.q: An LP is dissolved and its assets raise $10,000,000. Secured lenders are owed $6,000,000 and unsecured creditors are owed $3,500,000. How much is available for the limited partners and general partners combined?
w: Wrong: the claims total $9,500,000, which is less than $10,000,000, so something remains for partners.
Wrong: $1,000,000 would remain only if unsecured creditors were owed $3,000,000, but their claim is $3,500,000.
Wrong: this subtracts only the secured lenders’ $6,000,000 and forgets the general creditors’ claims.
Correct: lenders take $6,000,000, creditors $3,500,000, leaving $10,000,000 − $6,000,000 − $3,500,000 = $500,000 for the partners.

questions.q: Which is the correct order in which claims are satisfied on dissolution of a limited partnership? I. Limited partners II. Secured lenders III. General partners IV. General creditors
o: II, I, IV, III
IV, II, I, III
II, IV, I, III
II, IV, III, I
w: Wrong: this puts limited partners ahead of general creditors, but creditors come before any partner.
Wrong: this puts general creditors ahead of secured lenders, which reverses the first two ranks.
Correct: secured lenders, then general creditors, then limited partners, and finally general partners.
Wrong: this puts general partners ahead of limited partners, but general partners are always last.

questions.q: Which of the following is passed through to the partners of a qualifying limited partnership? I. Income II. Gains III. Losses IV. Depreciation and depletion deductions
o: I and II only
I, II, III and IV
I, II and III only
II, III and IV only
w: Wrong: this omits losses and deductions, which also pass through to partners.
Correct: the partnership is not a taxpayer, so income, gains, losses and deductions all flow to the partners.
Wrong: this omits the depreciation and depletion deductions, which are also passed through.
Wrong: this omits income, which is a core item passed through to each partner.

questions.q: A limited partnership drills for natural gas. Which tax deduction compensates it for using up the gas in the ground?
o: Depletion
Depreciation
Appreciation
Amortization of raw land
w: Correct: depletion is the deduction for using up a natural resource such as oil or gas.
Wrong: depreciation applies to the loss of value of hard assets like buildings, not natural resources.
Wrong: appreciation is a rise in an asset’s value, not a tax deduction, so it cannot compensate depletion.
Wrong: raw land is not a deductible hard asset and amortization is not the resource deduction described here.

questions.q: A limited partnership buys undeveloped land hoping to sell it later at a higher price. Which statement is correct?
o: The partnership may depreciate the land each year
The partnership may deplete the land like a natural resource
The land produces no value unless a building is built
The partnership cannot depreciate the land because raw land is not a hard asset; investors seek appreciation
w: Wrong: depreciation requires a hard asset, and raw land does not qualify.
Wrong: depletion is for natural resources such as oil and gas, and real estate cannot be depleted.
Wrong: land can appreciate without any building, which is the investors’ goal here.
Correct: raw land is not a hard asset, so it earns no depreciation, and investors rely on appreciation in value.

questions.q: A master limited partnership differs from a regular limited partnership in that an MLP
o: is offered to the public and traded on exchanges
gives its limited partners unlimited liability
is taxed as a C corporation
is never allowed to invest in natural resources
w: Correct: an MLP is a limited partnership whose interests are publicly offered and exchange-traded, so they are more liquid.
Wrong: MLP investors keep limited liability, much like corporate shareholders, so liability is not unlimited.
Wrong: MLPs pass income through, avoiding the double taxation of a C corporation.
Wrong: MLPs are particularly common in natural resources, financial services and real estate.

questions.q: Jack is considering an oil and gas limited partnership, and his representative suggests an oil and gas MLP instead. What advantage does the MLP offer that the regular LP lacks?
o: Pass-through of depletion deductions
Limited liability for investors
Avoidance of double taxation
Liquidity from exchange trading
w: Wrong: depletion deductions pass through in an ordinary LP as well, so this is not an MLP advantage.
Wrong: limited partners in a regular LP already have liability limited to their investment.
Wrong: both structures avoid double taxation because both are pass-through entities with no entity-level tax.
Correct: the MLP’s exchange trading gives liquidity; the tax and liability features are the same as in a regular LP.

questions.q: Which statement about MLPs is correct?
o: They are suitable only for institutional and accredited investors
They are subject to double taxation like a corporation
Because they are exchange-traded, they are more liquid and less risky than other DPPs and can suit retail investors
They must have a single limited partner
w: Wrong: that suitability limit describes illiquid non-traded DPPs in general, not exchange-traded MLPs.
Wrong: MLPs avoid double taxation through pass-through treatment of income, unlike a corporation.
Correct: exchange trading makes MLPs more liquid and suitable for a wider range of investors, including retail.
Wrong: MLPs may have hundreds of limited partners, so a single limited partner is not required.

questions.q: A hedge fund that charges “two and twenty” takes
o: a 20% annual management fee plus 2% of profits
a 2% annual management fee plus 20% of profits
a 2% sales charge for twenty years
a 2% fee for twenty months after purchase
w: Wrong: this reverses the percentages; the management fee is the smaller number.
Correct: two and twenty means roughly a 2% management fee on assets plus a 20% performance fee on profits.
Wrong: two and twenty is not a sales-charge schedule and has nothing to do with a twenty-year period.
Wrong: twenty does not refer to months; it is the percentage of profits taken as a performance fee.

questions.q: A hedge fund with $40,000,000 in assets earns a $5,000,000 profit for the year and charges two and twenty. What total fee does the manager earn?
w: Correct: the management fee is 2% × $40,000,000 = $800,000 and the performance fee is 20% × $5,000,000 = $1,000,000, totaling $1,800,000.
Wrong: $1,000,000 is only the performance fee and omits the 2% management fee of $800,000.
Wrong: this applies 2% and 20% to the wrong bases; 20% of the $5,000,000 profit is $1,000,000, not $2,000,000.
Wrong: this applies 20% to the whole asset base and 2% to profit, reversing the fee structure.

questions.q: Hedge fund managers are typically compensated by
o: a front-end sales charge only
a 12b-1 fee only
interest paid on a bond issued by the fund
an annual management fee based on assets and a performance fee based on increases in NAV
w: Wrong: a sales charge is not the hedge fund compensation model described in the chapter.
Wrong: a 12b-1 fee is not how hedge fund managers are paid in this structure.
Wrong: managers earn management and performance fees, not interest on a fund-issued bond.
Correct: hedge fund managers receive a management fee plus a performance fee, generally higher than fees on other funds.

questions.q: Which statement about hedge fund regulation is correct?
o: Hedge funds must register under the Investment Company Act of 1940
Hedge funds are exempt from anti-fraud provisions
Hedge funds are exempt from the Investment Company Act of 1940
Hedge fund managers owe no fiduciary duty to investors
w: Wrong: registration under the 1940 Act is exactly what hedge funds avoid.
Wrong: hedge funds are subject to the same fraud prohibitions as other market participants.
Correct: hedge funds are exempt from the 1940 Act, giving them flexibility in structure and design.
Wrong: hedge fund managers owe a fiduciary duty to the investors in their funds.

questions.q: Under the Dodd–Frank Act, which private fund manager must register with the SEC?
o: A manager of private funds with $100 million in assets
A manager of private funds with $200 million in assets
A manager of a fund with $150 million or less in assets
No private fund manager is required to register
w: Wrong: $100 million is below the $150 million threshold that triggers registration.
Correct: managers of private funds with more than $150 million in assets must register, and $200 million exceeds that threshold.
Wrong: the requirement applies above $150 million, so a fund at or below it is not caught.
Wrong: Dodd–Frank added provisions requiring larger private fund managers to register with the SEC.

questions.q: Which of the following strategies is characteristic of hedge funds and carries unlimited loss potential in rising markets?
o: Short selling
Buying securities for cash
Holding long positions only
Investing in a money market fund
w: Correct: short positions can lose an unlimited amount when prices rise, whereas a long position can fall only to zero.
Wrong: a cash purchase is a long position with loss capped at the amount invested.
Wrong: a long position can fall no further than zero, so loss is limited.
Wrong: a money market fund is a low-risk product and has no unlimited loss exposure.

questions.q: A hedge fund has a $250,000 minimum and a three-year lock-up. For which client need would it be LEAST appropriate?
o: Long-term capital appreciation
Diversification from stock and bond markets
Participation by a sophisticated, high-net-worth investor
Short-term access to cash
w: Wrong: a long-term investor is the type who can tolerate the lock-up period.
Wrong: hedge funds can provide returns not closely correlated with stocks and bonds, which supports this need.
Wrong: sophisticated high-net-worth investors are the intended hedge fund audience, so this need is a good fit.
Correct: a lock-up bars withdrawals, so a client who may need cash soon faces serious liquidity risk.

questions.q: The main risk created by a hedge fund lock-up period is
o: inflation risk
reinvestment risk
liquidity risk
call risk
w: Wrong: inflation risk is about purchasing power and is not what a lock-up creates.
Wrong: reinvestment risk is tied to reinvesting proceeds at lower rates, not to withdrawal restrictions.
Correct: investors cannot withdraw during the lock-up, so they face liquidity risk.
Wrong: call risk relates to bonds being redeemed early by the issuer.

questions.q: All of the following are differences between hedge funds and mutual funds EXCEPT
o: hedge funds may hold non-securities such as real estate
both are open to all investors, subject to the fund’s objectives
hedge funds use significant leverage while mutual funds have limited ability to trade on margin
hedge funds often impose a lock-up of two years or more
w: Wrong: holding non-securities such as real estate or jewelry is a genuine hedge fund difference.
Correct: only mutual funds are appropriate for all investors; hedge funds are limited to sophisticated high-net-worth investors.
Wrong: leverage including derivatives is a genuine hedge fund difference from mutual funds.
Wrong: lock-up periods of two years or more are a genuine hedge fund difference from redeemable mutual funds.

questions.q: Private equity funds generally invest
o: directly in private companies, often buying out or taking a majority position in a poorly performing business
in exchange-traded mortgage-backed securities
in a diversified portfolio of liquid government bonds
only in publicly traded shares at NAV
w: Correct: private equity funds put capital directly into private companies and work to turn them around, then exit by IPO or sale.
Wrong: holding MBS describes mortgage REIT activity and does not describe a private equity fund.
Wrong: private equity is high-risk and illiquid, not a portfolio of liquid government bonds.
Wrong: private equity targets private companies, not publicly traded shares at NAV.

questions.q: A private equity fund buys a majority position in a struggling manufacturer. Which statement about the fund’s investors and manager is correct?
o: Investors choose the company while the manager only collects fees
The manager is paid only if the fund’s shares trade on an exchange
The manager earns a fixed 20% of invested capital and no share of profits
Investors are passive while the manager performs due diligence and is paid about 2% of invested capital plus about 20% of profits
w: Wrong: investors play a passive role in selecting investments; the manager does the due diligence.
Wrong: private equity funds are not exchange-traded, and compensation is not tied to listing.
Wrong: the fee is roughly 2% of invested capital plus a portion of profits, not 20% of capital.
Correct: the management team researches and selects investments; investors are passive, and pay mirrors hedge fund fees.

questions.q: An exchange-traded note is best described as
o: a fund that owns the securities in its portfolio
a limited partnership offered to the public
an unsecured debt instrument of its issuer whose return is tied to an equity security or market
a pool issued by a state government
w: Wrong: owning the underlying securities is how an ETF works, not an ETN.
Wrong: that describes a master limited partnership, which is an LP and not a debt note like an ETN.
Correct: an ETN is unsecured corporate debt, typically issued by a broker-dealer, with a return tied to an underlying equity or market.
Wrong: that describes a municipal fund security, which is an equity pool and not a note like an ETN.

questions.q: An investor holds an ETN issued by a large investment bank, and the bank’s credit quality deteriorates sharply while the underlying stock index is unchanged. What is the most likely consequence?
o: No effect, since credit risk depends only on the index
The ETN loses value because its credit quality depends on the issuer, not the underlying
The ETN converts into shares of the underlying
The ETN becomes an ETF
w: Wrong: the note’s credit quality follows the issuer, not the underlying asset it tracks.
Correct: ETNs carry issuer credit risk, so the issuer’s weaker credit hurts the note even if the index is flat.
Wrong: an ETN is a debt instrument and does not convert into the underlying shares.
Wrong: an ETN cannot turn into an ETF; they are different structures.

questions.q: Which feature of an ETN is NOT found in an ETF?
o: A maturity date
Intraday trading on an exchange
The ability to track an index
The ability to buy a few shares at a time
w: Correct: ETNs are notes with a maturity date at which they are liquidated, while ETFs have no maturity.
Wrong: both ETNs and ETFs are exchange-traded products and can trade intraday.
Wrong: both products can seek to track an index, so this is not a unique ETN feature.
Wrong: both can be bought a few shares at a time on an exchange.

questions.q: Municipal fund securities are best described as
o: debt securities backed by a municipality’s taxing power
investment company shares regulated by the SEC
exchange-traded notes issued by a broker-dealer
equity investment pools issued by a state or local government entity
w: Wrong: unlike standard municipal securities, municipal fund securities are not debt securities.
Wrong: they are regulated by the MSRB and are not subject to SEC registration under the 1940 Act.
Wrong: an ETN is unsecured debt of a broker-dealer and has no connection to government pools.
Correct: municipal fund securities, defined in MSRB Rule D-12, are mutual-fund-like pools in which investors own a share, so they are equity.

questions.q: Which feature required of a mutual fund is NOT required of a local government investment pool?
o: Investment of pooled money by professional managers
Pooling of cash from many investors
Daily calculation of net asset value
A stated investment objective
w: Wrong: LGIP money is managed by government employees or an outside investment management firm.
Wrong: pooling money from many participants is the essence of an LGIP.
Correct: an LGIP is not required to calculate NAV daily, prepare a prospectus and SAI, or have independent directors.
Wrong: LGIPs operate under established investment objectives, such as stability or maximum return.

questions.q: A municipal securities dealer markets shares of an LGIP to a county treasurer. What must the dealer deliver, and when?
o: A prospectus, at or before the first contact
The issuer’s official statement, at or before settlement
The SEC registration statement, within 30 days
No document, because LGIPs are unregulated
w: Wrong: LGIPs are not SEC-registered mutual funds, so no prospectus is delivered; the disclosure is an official statement.
Correct: the dealer must obtain the issuer’s official statement and give it to the governmental investor at or before settlement.
Wrong: LGIPs are not subject to SEC registration, so no registration statement exists to deliver.
Wrong: LGIPs are regulated by the MSRB and are not unregulated; disclosure is required.
